- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.7) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to underreact — correct by adding 2–5% to forecast for short-term spikes.
- When sentiment is negative (e.g., <0.3) and forecast is rising, model often overestimates — correct by subtracting 2–5% for downward momentum.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast >85), model frequently overcorrects and underpredicts the next drop — adjust downward by 3–8% for 1–3 days post-spike.
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed (±0.3–0.7), model tends to smooth out extremes — correct by introducing a 1–3 day lag in mean reversion to avoid overcorrection.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often fails to capture long-term mean reversion — if sentiment is neutral or slightly negative, reduce forecast by 1–3% to align with historical mean.
- When sentiment is consistently positive over 3–5 days, model may overestimate future prices — apply a 1–3% downward bias to prevent overshoot.
- If forecast is rising steadily and sentiment is weakly positive, model may be too optimistic — reduce forecast slope by 0.5–1.5% per day to reflect sentiment lag.
